newsitem.title: USA: Teleglobe arms Bells for overseas calls.
newsitem.headline: Teleglobe arms Bells for overseas calls.

text.p: Three regional Bells, salivating over the potential of the $80 billion U.S. long-distance market, are arming themselves with an international calling capability through Canada's Teleglobe Inc., sources close to the deal said Tuesday.

Teleglobe has contracts with Ameritech Corp., BellSouth Corp. and Bell Atlantic Corp., which start with calling cards but are expected to expand to full international calling, sources close to the deals said.
On Wednesday, Chicago-based Ameritech will announce international calling card services using Teleglobe, the sources said.
The deals with the other two Bells will not be announced for several months, they say.

Ameritech will offer subscribers to its calling card the ability to call home or anywhere else from around the world. These calls are billed to the home phone. The cards also would allow collect calling from abroad.
None of the companies involved would comment.

"It does initially start with 1-800-AMERITECH, but as the company enters long distance Teleglobe will probably be one of the companies handling outbound international calling," one of the sources said, declining to be identified.
International calling is an essential weapon for regional Bells to have to grab large numbers of long-distance customers from AT&T Corp., MCI Communications Corp. and Sprint Corp., analysts say.

Regional Bells are allowed to enter the long-distance and international calling market as part of the 1996 Telecommunications Act, but only after they can show their local calling markets are competitive.

The sources said that Teleglobe's appeal to the Bells was its ability to provide a flexible package of services without having to worry that it was carving away at its own customer base as AT&T, MCI and Sprint would.
In providing these services it has become a competitor with Worldcom Inc., which has similar capabilities.

Teleglobe, which is 20 percent owned by Canada's BCE Inc., has annual revenues of about $1.2 billion and handles traffic for other telecommunications companies using its undersea cable and satellite systems.

Teleglobe's ambitions do not stop with serving the Bells. On Wednesday, it will announce an initiative to offer low-cost international calling to Fortune 500 businesses across the United States, the sources said.
These services include international private line, international voice, facsimile and global Internet access.
It will begin with New York, and by the end of the year will serve Atlanta, Chicago, Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles, Miami, Philadelphia, San Francisco and Washington.

Calling rates for businesses are 9.9 cents per minute from New York to Britain, peak or off-peak, with off-peak rates of 27 cents per minute for Germany, 29.5 cents for France, and 38.5 cents per minute for Japan, the sources say.
"Teleglobe will be going head-to-head with AT&T, MCI and many others," said another source.
